sections.heading: Why the Spring Visit Starts at the Outdoor Coil
body: The spring clean-and-check covers the condenser coil, electrical, refrigerant pressures, drains and the thermostat. Each one is a place an air conditioner fails on a hot day.

A dirty condenser coil makes the unit work harder to shed heat. Weak electrical parts keep a motor from starting, and a clogged drain can leave water where you don't want it. A spring check looks at each of them before the first hot week.

sections.heading: What Usually Stops a Furnace
body: The thermostat calls for heat and nothing happens, the furnace clicks and never lights, or it runs a minute and shuts down. A furnace goes through several steps before the house warms up, and a failure at any one of them stops the rest.

items.title: A worn igniter
items.text: The igniter lights the burner. When it cracks or weakens, the furnace tries to start and can't.

items.title: A dirty flame sensor
items.text: This small rod tells the furnace the flame is lit. Residue on it can shut the furnace down after a few seconds.

items.title: A clogged filter
items.text: Too little airflow makes a furnace overheat and shut itself off.

items.title: An inducer or blower motor
items.text: The inducer pulls exhaust out, and the blower pushes warm air through the house. When either fails, the heat doesn't arrive.

sections.heading: The Furnace Runs but the House Stays Cold
body: A furnace that runs and still leaves the rooms cold is a different problem from one that won't start. The cause might be airflow, a blower that isn't moving the warm air, or a thermostat telling the furnace the wrong thing.
Describe it the way you'd tell a neighbor: which rooms are cold, whether you can hear the blower, and how long it's been going on. That tells a technician where to start.

footer.about: Griffin HVAC is a Peoria heating and cooling company that has served the area since 1963, and has had its current owner since 2019. It repairs and installs furnaces and air conditioners, and sells a maintenance plan from $160 a year.
why: Plan members pay $75 for a service call

Your homepage headline reads “Please call if the online schedule doesn't show a time you want.” That is a notice, not an answer to what you do or where, and three different pages carry the title “Heating Services.” On a phone, every page is 768 pixels wide on a 390-pixel screen, so visitors scroll sideways, and the header shows Book Online and Log In but no phone number.

Your maintenance plan page is the best thing on your site. It prints a price, two visit checklists and a $75 service call with no after-hours, weekend or holiday rates. Today it hides behind the menu label “Maintenance Plan Agreement.”

So the demo leads with the plan, tells it the same way on every page, and opens with HVAC company in Peoria, IL. Furnace repair gets a page of its own, because it is where your customers and your plan meet.
